# Introduction

The eastern oyster (*Crassostrea virginica*) are viewed as a foundational species as they are directly responsible for creating and providing numerous ecosystem goods and services such as food and habitat production, shoreline stabilization and protection, water quality improvement, nutrient cycling, and carbon sequestration [@Geselbracht2024; @Grabowski2012; @Barnes2007]. Additionally, they provide numerous economic benefits such as supporting oyster fisheries, recreational harvesting, tourism, along with the associated employment that goes along with those  industries [@Geselbracht2024; @LaPeyre2021]. In one study, @Grabowski2012 estimated the average annual value to range from $10,325 to $99,421 per hectare (2011 Dollars).   

In recent decades, oyster reefs have experienced substantial declines, with only an estimated 15% remaining worldwide, and 50 to 80% being lost within the Gulf of (America) alone [@Pollack2012; @LaPeyre2021]. The decline is largely attributed to a combination of anthropogenic activities such us over harvesting, habitat alteration, sedimentation and water quality decline, disease and changing hydrology [@LaPeyre2021; @Geselbracht2024]. In response to these sharp declines, many restoration efforts have been undertaken with varying strategies and success rates; recently, planning documents released by the Deepwater Horizon Natural resource Damage Assessment Trustees called for large-scale development of reef networks to increase resilience [@Geselbracht2024]. 

## Oyster decline in the Pensacola Bay System

On such system to experience oyster decline is the Pensacola Bay System (PBS). The PBS is a large estuarine system located in Escambia and Santa Rosa counties in northwest Florida. The system is comprised of multiple waterbody's including Pensacola Bay, Escambia Bay, Blackwater Bay, East Bay, and Santa Rosa Sound; and is influenced heavily by freshwater input from the Escambia, Blackwater and Yellow Rivers [@Christensen1997]. Historically, the PBS supported extensive oyster reefs that provided critical habitat for a variety of species and substantial economic value to the surrounding communities [@Christensen1997]. However, over the past several decades, the extent of oyster habitat within the PBS has declined significantly due to a combination of factors including over harvesting, habitat degradation, and water quality issues. With some estimates indicating a decline of 15,000ha to just 91.5 ha of oyster habitat between the years of 1883 and 2021 [@Geselbracht2024]. This decline has prompted efforts to restore oyster reefs within the PBS [@PPBEP_OysterRestoration; @TNC2021OysterRestoration], with multiple studies aiming to identify the most suitable areas within the estuary to focus restoration efforts [@Geselbracht2024; @Christensen1997; @PPBEP_OysterRestoration].

With limited resources available for restoration, it is critical to identify areas where chances of oyster survival and long-term reef establishment are at their highest, and where poor site selection could ultimately lead to unsatisfactory results. As with any ecosystem, the environmental conditions within the PBS vary greatly in time and space, and such variations can have great impacts on oyster survival and establishment. Therefore, it is important to understand the environmental factors that drive oyster occurrence so that scientist and policy makers can make informed decisions regarding said restoration site selection [@Pollack2012; @Barnes2007; @Geselbracht2024].

## Environmental controls on Eastern oyster habitat

Oyster recruitment, survival, and reef establishment are influenced by complex interactions between numerous physical, chemical, and biological environmental factors. As such, determining the most influential factors is a multivariate problem that requires careful consideration of each factor and its interactions with others [@LaPeyre2021; @Pollack2012; @Barnes2007; @Christensen1997]. To help narrow the focus, the most commonly cited environmental factors were examined in the literature and are summarized here. 
   
Perhaps the most influential and widely reported environmental driver of oyster suitability is salinity. Representing an important environmental gradient within estuarine systems that influences physiology, recruitment, disease, predation, and survival. Other important characteristics often reported can be seen in @tbl-environmental-drivers and include: dissolved oxygen, temperature, depth, turbidity, and bottom type (substrate) [@LaPeyre2021; @Pollack2012; @Barnes2007; @Geselbracht2024; @Christensen1997].

It should be recognized that not all environmental factors are adequately spatially distributed or represented within the available datasets, and therefore careful consideration should be given when selecting the final dataset used for modeling habitat suitability [@LaPeyre2021; @Geselbracht2024; @Christensen1997].

## Species Distribution Modelling

Quantifying the relationships between the distribution of species and the species-environment interactions have a long history in ecological research, having been described as far back as the late 17th early 18th century in which researchers observed biological patterns in terms of their relationships with geographical and/or environmental gradients [@Rushton2004; @Elith2009]. Since then, the propagation of large-scale spatial datasets, the development and integration of GIS, increased access to statistical packages and computational power have allowed for much more development in modeling complex species-environment interactions [@Johnson2005]. Out of such developments has arisen a technique known as Species Distribution Modeling (SDM), which can be loosely defined as numerical tools that combine observations of species occurrence or abundance with environmental estimates [@Elith2009]. According to @Elith2009, SDMs can be largely classified within several families of models: expert-driven or heuristic, environmental-envelope, environmental-similarity, regression-based, Bayesian and hierarchical, machine-learning and data mining, and ensemble or multimodal. Additionally, the selection of an SDM approach largely depends on a multitude of factors such as: the study's objective, quality and quantity of available data, ecological characteristics of the species, spatial and temporal scale, whether input data includes absence data or presence-only data [@Elith2009]. With so many choices of modeling technique and the driving factors behind that choice, deciding on one model can be quite difficult and the choice usually defaults to a standard technique depending on the subject matter. 

*Habitat Suitability Indices*

One popular approach used in many studies involving the Eastern oyster throughout the gulf region is that of the expert-driven Habitat Suitability Index [@Barnes2007; @Pollack2012; @Geselbracht2024; @Christensen1997]. HSIs are typically used in situations where quantitative data on species distributions is difficult to collect or non-existent, relying on expert-driven variable selection, meta-analysis, and classification methods that transform environmental characteristics into standardized estimates of habitat suitability [@Barnes2007; @Pollack2012; @Geselbracht2024; @Johnson2005]. 

Within the PBS, HSIs have been used to develop GIS-based and estuary-specific HSMs that integrate biological, physical, chemical, and management-related variables in order to identify suitable restoration areas with the system. In the mid 1990's @Christensen1997 developed a HSI for the eastern oyster in the PBS to demonstrate the model frameworks usefulness in illustrating species suitability in a system wide approach. @Geselbracht2024 then followed and further expanded on the approach incorporating management factors into the model, adding a layer of regulatory influence to the model output versus the purely environmental analysis of the prior. Additionally, the Pensacola and Perdido Bay Estuary Program recently built on-top of @Geselbracht2024 by incorporating some of their own data and refining some of the weighting [@PPBEP_OysterRestoration]. 

These previous studies alone highlight the strengths and weakness of the HSI approaches. Some of the strengths include interoperability, adaptability, and the integration of ecological knowledge, but the results entirely rely on expert decisions regarding variable selection, suitability functions, weighting and scoring, and how to aggregate the results. All of these present opportunity for differing outputs even if the same inputs were used by different groups [@Geselbracht2024; @Johnson2005].

*Maximum Entropy Modelling (MaxEnt)*

MaxEnt is a presence-background SDM framework based on general-purpose machine learning methods that are useful for making predictions using incomplete information by relating environmental conditions at known occurrence locations to the environmental conditions throughout the study area [@Phillips2006; @Elith2011]. Some of the main benefits of MaxEnt is that it uses presence-only data, reducing the need for the often un-available absence data, it has the ability to model complex interactions between environmental conditions, and it has demonstrated high predictive performance while limiting over fitting through regularization [@Phillips2009; @Merow2013; @Elith2011]. An added benefit to this particular study is the fact that MaxEnt is tailored towards presence-only species occurrence data, making it highly suitable for the data set used here in which the @FWC2026Oysters datasets explicitly collected occurrence data without including absence locations.  

However, the use of such algorithms should not be made blindly as many issues can arise if careful precautions are not taken. Due to the nature of ecological many biases in the data samples can arise such as spatial and temporal autocorrelation, group dependence structures, hierarchical structures and multicollinearity leading to overfitting model parameters and over-optimistic prediction confidence [@Dormann2013; @Kass2021; @Roberts2017]. Thankfully, significant work has been put into this through cross-validation techniques and the development of model evaluation software packages such as ENMeval 2.0 implemented through the R statistical language [@Kass2021; @Roberts2017]

To demonstrate how a MaxEnt SDM can be used as a complimentary tool to help researchers and practitioners leading ecological restoration activities, this study aims to develop an empirically fitted MaxEnt habitat-suitability model using observed oyster occurrence data and known environmental conditions. The primary objective will be to develop a spatially explicit SDM representing relative Eastern oyster habitat suitabiliy throughout the PBS. Next, the resulting suitability surface will be evaluated agains the existing Pensacola Bay HSI developed by @Geselbracht2024 and iterated upon by @PPBEP_OysterRestoration. To achieve this, environmental predictors that are commonly associated with oyster habitat suitability will be identified and obtained. The predictors will be used to fit the MaxEnt model and model performance will be evaluated using spatially separated cross-validation. Finally, we will compare the predicted surface to the existing HSI to determine areas of agreement and disagreement, and we will use these results to determine whether the MaxEnt framework provides an empirical alternative or compliment to HSI-based restoration planning. It is hypothesized that the MaxEnt model will successfully identify patterns of habitat suitability for the Easter oyster withinthe PBS. Overall agreement between the HSI and MaxEnt is expected to be high. However, MaxEnt is expected to produce a smoother, more continuous suitability surface because of the empirically fitted environmental relationships as opposed to predefined, lower-resolution HSI suitability envelopes. As a result, the MaxEnt model could prove beneficial to help narrow down project locations to help reinforce expert-driven model outputs.  



# Methods

All data analysis and processing was performed using the R programming language [@r]. Environmental observation data was acquired from the EPA's Water Quality Portal via the dataRetrieval r-package [@wqp_2026; @dataRetrieval2026]. Data QA/QC and preprocessing was completed utilizing the Tidyverse package and any spatially aware data processing was conducted using the package sf [@tidyverse; @sf]. All spatial data was projected to the NAD83 / Florida North State Plane Coordinate System (EPSG: 2238) which minimizes spatial distortion in the study areas geographic region. 

**Study Area**

The study area for this project is the Pensacola Bay System which includes portions of Pensacola Bay, Escambia Bay, East Bay and Blackwater Bay. Boundaries of this study area were achieved by accessing Florida Department of Protections (FDEP) Waterbod IDs feature layer hosted on ArcGIS Online [@FDEP2005WBIDs]. Once retrieved, the dataset was filtered to include only relevant WBIDs (WBID = 548) and then combined to create a singular study area polygon. Creating the study area polygon is an important first step as it was needed to extract relevant environmental data from much larger datasets in the coming data gathering. The study area was intentionally chosen in an attempt to match the previous study area applied in @Geselbracht2024. 

![Study area for the Pensacola Bay System.](4-tables-and-figures/fig-1-study_area.png){#fig-study-area}

**Data Acquisition and Processing**

Oyster occurence data was acquired from the Florida Fish and Wildlife Commission's GIS portal as polygons and converted to points using polygon centroids. After clipping to the study area extent, ### known reef locations were present within the PBS [@FWC2026Oysters]. Salinity, dissolved oxygen, temperature, and turbidity, and chlorophyll-a observations were obtained from the Water Quality Portal using the 'dataRetrieval' package in R for all sites located within the PBS and collected within the 20 year period from 2005 to 2025 [@wqp_2026, @dataRetrieval2026]. Parameters were chosen based on relevance and represenation in previous oyster habitat retoration studies [@LaPeyre2021; @Barnes2007; @Pollack2012; @Geselbracht2024]. Bathymetry data for the PBS was obtained from NOAA as a **####** resolution raster dataset [@NOAA_2018]. **DOES BATHYMETRY DATA NEED TO BE RESAMPLED TO NEW CELL SIZE?**. Substrate data was obtained from the Pensacola and Perdido Bay Estuary Program and was the same dataset used in their earlier HSI study which was modeled on the @Geselbracht2024 study.

**Water-quality Data Preprocessing**

All water quality parameters were inspected to ensure comparable measurement units and analytical procedures and avoid combining different forms of similar analytes. Further, to maintain consistency with other similar oyster studies, all data was filtered to only include warm season conditions. Here, the warm season is defined as any data that was collected in the monthes of May, June, July, August, September, or October. Finally, the data was screened for any extreme outliers, where outliers were defined as:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Outlier if } \quad
x &< Q_{0.25} - 1.5(IQR) \\
\text{or} \quad
x &> Q_{0.75} + 1.5(IQR) \\
\\
\text{where } IQR &= Q_{0.75} - Q_{0.25}
\end{aligned}
$$

To avoid spatial bias during the interpolation process, station-level site data was aggregated using 2000m hexagonal spatial bins, taking the mean value of all data within that bin and returning a single value for each hexagon, using the hexagons centroid as the representative point for the data value. Stations that only had one sample were removed as was considered one sample was not representative enough to be considered the normal conditions over the full 20 year period.   

### Environmental Prediction Rasters

Continuous prediction rasters were generated for dissolved oxygen, salinity, turbidity, and water temperature using Inverse Path Distance Weighting (IPDW) package in R [@IPDW_2023]. IPDW is a variant of Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW), which is a deterministic interpolation method that allows for the estimation of point values using the equation:

$$ 
V= \frac{\sum\limits^{n}_{i=1} v_i {d^{-p}_{i}}}{\sum\limits^{n}_{i=1} {d^{-p}_{i}}} 
$$

where $d$ is the distance between the prediction and measurement points, $v_i$ is the parameter value, and $p$ is a power parameter. However, in IPDW $d$ is a calculated path-distance value rather than a typical euclidean distance as used in IDW [@Stachelek2015]. 

 IPDW was selected due to its ability to be barrier aware and avoid interference or influence from crossing land boundaries that can be introduced when using more traditional euclidean based interpolation methods [@Stachelek2015]. This is especially important given the geography on PBS where the Garcon Point area is a narrow, low lying peninsula separating Escambia Bay to the west and Blackwater Bay to the east. Both of which are significantly influence by different riverine inputs. Instead, IPDW weights observations according to the shortest water-path distance through the aquatic environment. Chlorophyll-a was also evaluated, but was ultimately removed due to lack of spatial and temporal representation. 

*Creation of the cost-distance raster*

Monitoring site locations were used to define the interpolation domain for each of the environmental variables using the spatial extent. A land-barrier polygon was created by taking the inverse of the study area polygon. To achieve this, a singular polygon was created using the entire study area extent bounding box and adding 1,000 meters to each side ensuring full coverage. Next the PBS study-area polygon geometry was subtracted from the study area extent polygon. Leaving behind a land barrier polygon that would be used to create the path-distance calculations for the IPDW algorithm.  

An IPDW cost raster was then calculated using the monitoring site locations as point data and the newly created land-barrier polygon as the barrier geometry. The raster was the converted to 100m resolution and projected to the Florida North State Plane CRS to align with other spatial data. 

*IPDW parameter sensitivity analysis*

All parameter IPDW models were evaluated for sensitivity to determine influence of distance power and maximum path distance on overall interpolation performance. In IPDW, distance power determines how rapid the site influence decays as path distance increases. The distance powers ($p$) tested were: 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00, 1.25, 1.50, 2.00, 2.50 and 3.00. The influence of maximum path distance was also evaluated for each IPDW model, in which the maximum range determines the max distance in which a measured value can contribute to the prediction value. Maximum ranges evaluated were: 5km, 10km, 15km, and 20km. All combinations of distance power and maximum range values were evaluated to determine the best fit for each parameter allowing for tuned parameter to be chosen empirically rather than by assumption. However, in many situations the diagnostics proved a range of plausible values, in which case the smother gradient was chosen as the PBS is a well mixed system and some parameter combinations would result in generating surfaces that contained "bulls-eyes" in which the parameter would highly influence the immediate area causing for ecologically implausible surfaces. 

Spatial cross-validation was used to determine interpolation accuracy using the blockCV package in R, which uses spatial folds to split data into test and training data sets [@Valavi2019]. To improve fitting, the fold-generation procedure was repeated, each time refitting the IPDW model and comparing the results to the with-held observation spatial-blocks. For this analysis 5 spatial folds were used with 5km spatial blocks, and blocks were assigned the folds randomly. This process was then repeated across 5 random seeds in which a new spatial partition was generated for each seed. For each spatial fold, the monitoring locations were used in the training data to construct the IPDW prediction surface. Withheld monitoring locations were used to extract predicted values from the prediction raster and compared to the observed station means. 

Finally, model performance was evaluated using calculated prediction-error statistics for each DP-MR combination. Each statistic was summarized across each repetition to generate a mean Mean Absolute Error (MAE), the standard deviation of the MAE, the mean Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) and its standard deviation, the mean prediction bias (+/-) and finally the prediction coverage. Mean MAE was the primary metric used in parameter selection, although in cases were differences between several of the lowest results were negligible, the smoother surfaces were given preference to better reflect the reality of a well mixed natural system. 

*Final Prediction Raster Generation*

The final prediction surfaces were generated by fitting the IPDW algorithm using the selected DP and MR values on the full dataset for each environmental variable. A new path-distance raster was also created using the selected maximum range value from the sensitivity analysis. The final prediction surfaces were validated using a reproducible known seed, 5km spatial blocks, and five folds to calculate the final MAE, RMSE, prediction bias, and prediction coverage.
